To determine the conditions under which the composition \( f \circ g \) is surjective, we analyze the requirements on both functions \( f \) and \( g \).

1. **Surjectivity of \( g \)**:
   - For \( f \circ g \) to be surjective, every element in the codomain of \( f \) must be mapped to by some element in the domain of \( g \). This requires \( g \) to be surjective because if \( g \) were not surjective, there would exist elements in the codomain of \( f \) that \( g \) could not map to, making \( f \circ g \) non-surjective.

2. **Non-constant Image of \( f \)**:
   - The function \( f \) must not map all elements to a single value. If \( f \) were constant (i.e., its image is a singleton), then \( f \circ g \) would also be constant, hence not surjective. Therefore, \( f \) must be such that its image is not a singleton.

Combining these conditions, we conclude that \( g \) must be surjective and \( f \) must not have a constant image (i.e., it must not map all inputs to a single output).

### Final Answer
\boxed{g \text{ is surjective and } f \text{ is not constant}}

   - For \( f \circ g \) to be surjective, every element in the codomain of \( f \) must be mapped to by some element in the domain of \( g \).    - The function \( f \) must not map all elements to a single value. If \( f \) were constant (i.e., its image is a singleton), then \( f \circ g \) would also be constant, hence not surjective. Therefore, \( f \) must be such that its image is not a singleton.
